title: The oldest poems
hookLine: among the oldest Buddhist verses, first put into English in full in 1881

cards: In 1881, in Oxford, a volume came off the press: the tenth book in a series called the Sacred Books of the East. Inside were two Buddhist texts in English, side by side. One was the Dhammapada, translated by Max Muller.
The other was a collection of poems, translated from the Pali by a Danish scholar named Viggo Fausboll. Some readers think a few of those poems belong to the oldest layers of the Buddhist canon.
Today, that second book opens. Today's word: Sutta Nipata.

teach.b: Sutta Nipata means something like the collection of discourses, or the gathering of suttas.
It's a small book of short pieces, most of them in verse, sorted into five chapters. Some you may have met: the discourse on loving-kindness, the discourse on blessings, the rhinoceros poem.
Why do some scholars call parts of it old? The language of some verses is archaic, closer to older Indian poetry.
The fourth and fifth chapters, the Chapter of Eights and the Way to the Beyond, are explained line by line by another text inside the canon itself, the Niddesa.
To these scholars, a commentary inside the canon suggests the poems were already old and already puzzling while the canon was still being shaped.
And the life in them is spare: wanderers, forests, rivers, almost no buildings, very little organization. Some read that as a window onto the earliest days.
Others are more cautious and say old verses and newer ones sit side by side. So this path reads it slowly.

teach.h: POEMS MEANT TO BE SAID ALOUD
teach.b: These are poems meant to be said aloud and remembered, with refrains that come back verse after verse, the way a song comes back to its chorus.
Ahead: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros, a plowman, a spirit with a threat, and a long list of blessings.

how: Verses from the Sutta Nipata, especially the discourses on loving-kindness, blessings and the jewel, are among the texts chanted in Theravada temples and homes, and the collection is studied in monasteries.

practice: Read one verse aloud, from the other book in that 1881 volume, Max Muller's Dhammapada, a line that calls itself old.
Say it slowly, in a normal speaking voice: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love; this is an old rule.
Say it once more, a little slower, and notice the sound in your mouth and the quiet after it, then sit with the breath.
